topics.title: Polynomials
topics.description: Polynomials, their degrees and zeroes, and the remainder and factor theorems.

lessons.title: Polynomials, Degrees and Zeroes
objectives: Identify polynomials in one variable
Classify polynomials by degree and number of terms
Evaluate a polynomial for a given value
Find zeroes of linear polynomials and verify zeroes
lessons.intro: Expressions such as 3x² − 5x + 2 appear throughout mathematics and science: in the path of a thrown ball, the area of a garden, or the profit of a business. Such expressions are called polynomials. A polynomial in one variable x is an expression made of terms of the form axⁿ, where a is a real number and n is a whole number. Understanding their structure lets us evaluate them, find when they become zero and factorise them.
sections: What is a polynomial?

A polynomial in x is a sum of terms such as 4x³, −2x and 7, where the exponents of x are whole numbers (0, 1, 2, …). Expressions with negative or fractional exponents, or with x in a denominator or under a square root, are not polynomials: x⁻¹ + 2, √x + 1 and 1/x are not polynomials. The numbers multiplying the powers of x are coefficients. A constant such as 9 is a polynomial of degree 0, and the zero polynomial 0 has no defined degree.
Degree and types

The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of the variable with a non-zero coefficient. In 5x³ − 2x² + x − 8 the degree is 3. Polynomials of degree 1 are linear (2x + 3), of degree 2 quadratic (x² − 4x + 1), and of degree 3 cubic. By number of terms, a polynomial with one term is a monomial (7x²), two terms a binomial (x + 5) and three terms a trinomial (x² + x + 1). The general linear polynomial is ax + b with a ≠ 0, and the general quadratic is ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0.
Value and zeroes

We write a polynomial as p(x). Its value at x = a is p(a), found by substituting a: if p(x) = x² − 3x + 2, then p(4) = 16 − 12 + 2 = 6. A zero (or root) of p(x) is a number c for which p(c) = 0. For p(x) above, p(1) = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0 and p(2) = 4 − 6 + 2 = 0, so 1 and 2 are zeroes. A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, x = −b/a. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes, and a non-zero constant polynomial has none.
definitions: An expression of terms axⁿ where n is a whole number.
The highest power of the variable with a non-zero coefficient.
The number multiplying a power of the variable.
A value of the variable that makes the polynomial equal to 0.
examples: p(y) = 4y³ − y + 6 is a cubic trinomial.

lessons.title: Remainder and Factor Theorems
objectives: Divide a polynomial by a linear polynomial
Use the remainder theorem to find remainders quickly
Use the factor theorem to test and find factors
Factorise quadratic and cubic polynomials
lessons.intro: Dividing 17 by 5 gives quotient 3 and remainder 2, because 17 = 5 × 3 + 2. Polynomials can be divided in the same way. Two powerful results, the remainder theorem and the factor theorem, let us find remainders and factors without doing long division. These ideas are the key to factorising cubic polynomials and solving higher-degree equations.
sections: Division and the remainder theorem

When a polynomial p(x) is divided by a non-zero polynomial g(x), we get p(x) = g(x) × q(x) + r(x), where q(x) is the quotient and r(x) the remainder, with the remainder of lower degree than g(x). The remainder theorem says: if p(x) is divided by the linear polynomial (x − a), the remainder is p(a). For example, dividing p(x) = x³ − 2x + 1 by (x − 2) gives remainder p(2) = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5. To divide by (x + 3), use a = −3; to divide by (2x − 1), use a = 1/2.
The factor theorem

The factor theorem follows directly: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0. In other words, a is a zero of p(x) exactly when (x − a) divides p(x) with no remainder. For p(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, p(1) = 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor. To find integer zeroes of a polynomial with integer coefficients and leading coefficient 1, test the factors of the constant term: here ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6.
Factorising

Quadratics ax² + bx + c can be factorised by splitting the middle term: find two numbers whose product is ac and whose sum is b. For 2x² + 7x + 3, ac = 6, and 6 + 1 = 7, so 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3). For a cubic, find one factor using the factor theorem, divide to get a quadratic, then factorise the quadratic. For x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, dividing by (x − 1) gives x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so the polynomial is (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry and Linear Equations
topics.description: The Cartesian plane and linear equations in two variables with their graphs.

lessons.title: The Cartesian Plane
objectives: Describe the x-axis, y-axis, origin and quadrants
Plot points given their coordinates
Identify the quadrant or axis on which a point lies
Find the distance between points on a horizontal or vertical line
lessons.intro: How do you tell a friend exactly where a seat is in a cinema hall? You give the row and the seat number. In the seventeenth century the French mathematician René Descartes used the same idea to locate any point on a flat surface with two numbers. This system, the Cartesian plane, joins algebra and geometry: equations can be drawn as graphs, and shapes can be studied using numbers.
sections: Axes and coordinates

Two perpendicular number lines meet at the origin O. The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis. Every point P is described by an ordered pair (x, y). The x-coordinate (abscissa) is its distance from the y-axis, measured along the x-axis, positive to the right and negative to the left. The y-coordinate (ordinate) is its distance from the x-axis, positive upwards and negative downwards. The origin is (0, 0). Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
Quadrants and axes

The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise from the upper right. In Quadrant I both coordinates are positive (+, +); in Quadrant II (−, +); in Quadrant III (−, −); and in Quadrant IV (+, −). A point on the x-axis has y = 0, such as (4, 0) or (−3, 0), and a point on the y-axis has x = 0, such as (0, −6). Points on the axes do not belong to any quadrant. To plot (−3, 2), move 3 units left from the origin and then 2 units up.
Using coordinates

Coordinates allow us to describe shapes precisely. The points A(1, 1), B(5, 1), C(5, 4) and D(1, 4) form a rectangle. Distances along horizontal or vertical lines are easy to find: AB lies on the line y = 1, so AB = |5 − 1| = 4 units; BC lies on x = 5, so BC = |4 − 1| = 3 units. The area of the rectangle is 4 × 3 = 12 square units. All points with the same x-coordinate lie on a vertical line, and all points with the same y-coordinate lie on a horizontal line.
definitions: The point (0, 0) where the axes meet.
One of the four regions into which the axes divide the plane.
A pair (x, y) in which the order of the numbers matters.

lessons.title: Linear Equations in Two Variables
objectives: Write linear equations in two variables from situations
Find solutions of a linear equation in two variables
Draw the graph of a linear equation
Interpret equations of lines parallel to the axes
lessons.intro: If a pen costs ₹x and a notebook costs ₹y, and together they cost ₹50, we can write x + y = 50. Unlike equations with one variable, this has many solutions: (10, 40), (25, 25), (35, 15) and so on. An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a and b are not both zero, is a linear equation in two variables. All its solutions, when plotted, lie on a straight line.
sections: Solutions

A solution of a linear equation in two variables is an ordered pair (x, y) that satisfies it. For 2x + y = 7, the pair (1, 5) is a solution because 2(1) + 5 = 7, and (3, 1) is also a solution. To find solutions, choose a convenient value for one variable and solve for the other: if x = 0, y = 7; if y = 0, x = 3.5. Such an equation has infinitely many solutions, because for every value of x there is a matching y.
Drawing the graph

To draw the graph of 2x + y = 7, find at least two (preferably three) solutions, plot them and join them with a straight line: for example (0, 7), (2, 3) and (3, 1). The third point is a check: if it does not lie on the line, there is a mistake. Every point on the line is a solution, and every solution lies on the line. The line crosses the y-axis where x = 0 and the x-axis where y = 0. The graph of y = mx passes through the origin.
Special lines and applications

The equation y = 3 represents a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis, 3 units above it, because every point on it has y-coordinate 3 whatever x is. Similarly, x = −2 is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis. The x-axis itself is y = 0 and the y-axis is x = 0. Linear equations model many real situations: if a taxi charges ₹50 plus ₹15 per km, the fare y for x km is y = 15x + 50. Its graph lets us read off the fare for any distance.
definitions: An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, with a and b not both zero.
An ordered pair (x, y) that satisfies the equation.
The set of all points whose coordinates satisfy it.
The point where a line crosses an axis.

topics.title: Triangles
topics.description: Congruence of triangles and finding area using Heron's formula.

lessons.title: Congruence of Triangles
objectives: Explain what congruent figures are
State and apply the SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS congruence rules
Use CPCT to prove parts equal
Prove properties of isosceles triangles
lessons.intro: Two photocopies of the same page, two coins of the same value or two identical tiles fit exactly on each other. Figures that have exactly the same shape and size are congruent. For triangles, we do not need to check all six parts (three sides and three angles) to know they are congruent; a few carefully chosen parts are enough. These shortcuts, the congruence rules, are the basis of many proofs in geometry.
sections: Congruence and correspondence

Triangles ABC and PQR are congruent, written △ABC ≅ △PQR, if they can be made to coincide exactly, with A on P, B on Q and C on R. The order of letters shows which parts correspond: AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP, ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and ∠C = ∠R. Once two triangles are proved congruent, all their corresponding parts are equal; this is written CPCT (corresponding parts of congruent triangles).
Congruence rules

SAS: two sides and the included angle of one triangle equal those of the other. ASA: two angles and the included side are equal. AAS: two angles and any non-included side are equal (because the third angles must then be equal too). SSS: all three sides are equal. RHS: in right triangles, the hypotenuse and one other side are equal. Note that SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) and AAA (three angles) are NOT congruence rules: AAA triangles have the same shape but may differ in size.
Isosceles triangles

Congruence lets us prove important results. In an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, draw the bisector AD of ∠A. In △ABD and △ACD, AB = AC, ∠BAD = ∠CAD and AD is common, so △ABD ≅ △ACD by SAS. By CPCT, ∠B = ∠C. So angles opposite equal sides are equal. The converse is also true: sides opposite equal angles are equal. Also from the same congruence, BD = DC and ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, so the bisector of the vertex angle is the perpendicular bisector of the base.

The angle between two given sides.

The side opposite the right angle in a right triangle.

lessons.title: Area of a Triangle: Heron's Formula
objectives: Recall the area of a triangle using base and height
Compute the semi-perimeter of a triangle
Use Heron's formula to find the area from three sides
Find areas of quadrilaterals by splitting them into triangles
lessons.intro: The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, but in real life the height is often hard to measure. Imagine a triangular park whose sides you can pace out, but where you cannot easily draw a perpendicular height across the grass. Heron of Alexandria, a mathematician of the first century, found a formula that gives the area using only the lengths of the three sides.
sections: Semi-perimeter

For a triangle with sides a, b and c, the perimeter is a + b + c and the semi-perimeter s is half of it: s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2. For a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm, s = 42 ÷ 2 = 21 cm. Notice that s − a, s − b and s − c must all be positive; this is equivalent to the triangle inequality, which says that the sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side. If it fails, no triangle exists.
Heron's formula

Heron's formula states: Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]. For the 13-14-15 triangle: s − a = 8, s − b = 7, s − c = 6, so Area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7,056 = 84 cm². Breaking numbers into prime factors before taking the square root often makes calculation easier: 21 × 8 × 7 × 6 = (3 × 7) × 2³ × 7 × (2 × 3) = 2⁴ × 3² × 7², whose square root is 2² × 3 × 7 = 84. For an equilateral triangle of side a, the formula gives (√3/4)a².
Quadrilaterals and applications

Any quadrilateral can be divided by a diagonal into two triangles. If we know the four sides and one diagonal, we can find both triangles' areas with Heron's formula and add them. For example, a quadrilateral field ABCD with AB = 9 m, BC = 40 m, CD = 28 m, DA = 15 m and diagonal AC = 41 m splits into △ABC (9, 40, 41), which is right-angled with area 180 m², and △ACD (41, 28, 15), whose area by Heron's formula is 126 m². The total area is 306 m².
definitions: Half the perimeter of a triangle: s = (a + b + c)/2.
Area of a triangle = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third.
A triangle with all sides of different lengths.
examples: A triangle with sides 5, 12, 13 has s = 15 and area √(15 × 10 × 3 × 2) = 30.
An equilateral triangle of side 6 cm has area (√3/4) × 36 ≈ 15.6 cm².
